newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong Chinese rush for consular protection.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong Chinese rush for consular protection.

text.p: Worried about their safety under Beijing's rule, thousands of Hong Kong Chinese carrying foreign passports rushed to secure consular protection on Wednesday.
In just six days, Hong Kong will become part of China, which does not accept dual nationality.
Beijing has declared it will treat all ethnic Chinese residents as Chinese nationals.
Unless overseas passport holders declare their nationalities to immigration authorities, they will not be entitled to consular protection.
"I don't want to take any risks," said Canadian Peter Lau, waiting in line outside an immigration office.
"I'm used to living in places which have a good rule of law, but what I fear the most is there's no such concept in China."
"I feel there are still many uncertainties in the future Hong Kong and I'm always prepared to fly back to Canada if there are any changes."
Hundreds of thousands of Hong Kong people have migrated to the West since Britain and China signed an agreement in 1984 on the handover of the territory.
Many left after China's bloody military crackdown on the student-led pro-democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June, 1989.
But some have returned, with foreign passports in their pockets, to find higher-paying jobs.

"We're seeking more protection and that's why my family and I left Hong Kong eight years ago," said Karen Chan, who migrated to Australia after the massacre but has returned to run a jewellery business.
Around 7,000 returnees picked up declaration forms on Tuesday, the first day they were made available, an immigration spokesman said.
